summary: This bill amends 28 U.S.C. 1346(a) to give district courts original and concurrent jurisdiction over suits against the United States to undo termination of a federal grant when the termination arises from an agency action already under APA review in chapter 7 of title 5.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a) to grant district courts original and concurrent jurisdiction over civil actions seeking to vacate the termination of federal grants when those terminations are tied to agency actions reviewable under the APA (chapter 7 of title 5). This creates a new procedural avenue for plaintiffs to challenge and potentially reverse grant terminations, thereby protecting existing federal expenditures from being cut. It does not authorize new spending but makes terminations harder to sustain, producing a moderate negative effect on efforts to reduce government spending.
The bill addresses only federal-court jurisdiction over grant-termination disputes and contains no provisions altering tax rates, tax policy, or revenue collection.
The legislation is limited to procedural rules for challenging grant terminations and does not address healthcare delivery, insurance markets, or public versus private coverage models.
No provisions in the bill relate to firearms regulation, Second Amendment rights, or enforcement mechanisms.
The bill does not modify immigration statutes, border policy, or pathways to legal status.
Nothing in the text concerns reproductive-health services, funding restrictions, or access to abortion.
While federal grants could theoretically include defense-related awards, the bill is a general jurisdictional rule and does not direct or alter military or defense appropriations.
The measure contains no environmental regulatory changes or conservation provisions.
Although some grants might support safety-net programs, the bill itself is strictly procedural and does not expand or contract eligibility or funding levels for welfare programs.
No language addresses school funding formulas, school choice, or federal education policy.
The bill does not touch drug enforcement, decriminalization, or related criminal statutes.
Jurisdiction over grant-termination suits has no bearing on sentencing, policing, or rehabilitation policy.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions appear in the text.
By facilitating judicial challenges to grant terminations, the bill could indirectly preserve federal outlays and thereby slow deficit reduction; the connection is indirect and modest.
The legislation is silent on civil-rights protections or legal status for LGBTQ+ individuals.
Although some federal grants involve foreign assistance, the bill creates only a general jurisdictional rule and does not change foreign-aid policy or funding.
No election-administration, voting-access, or campaign-finance provisions are present.
The bill does not regulate technology companies, data practices, or privacy standards.
Nothing in the text addresses collective bargaining, worker protections, or union authority.
The measure contains no provisions balancing religious exemptions against anti-discrimination requirements.
